overview:
In Jain philosophy, the "substantial standpoint" is usually referred to by the Sanskrit/Prakrit term "dravyanaya" – the standpoint that focuses on the enduring substance (dravya) rather than its changing modes (paryāya). It is one of the principal philosophical perspectives (naya) used to analyze reality within the broader doctrine of anekāntavāda, the Jain teaching that reality is complex and can be understood from multiple, non-exclusive viewpoints. From the substantial standpoint, a thing is considered primarily in terms of what it essentially is: its underlying, persistent nature and its fundamental qualities (guṇa) that remain through change.

Jain metaphysics holds that all real entities are substances (dravya) endowed with qualities (guṇa) and modes (paryāya). A substance is eternal in the sense that it does not come into existence from absolute non-being nor pass into absolute non-being; instead, it continuously undergoes modifications while retaining its identity. The substantial standpoint emphasizes this continuity and identity. For example, a soul (jīva) remains a soul through countless births and deaths, even though its states—ignorant or enlightened, embodied or liberated—change. Similarly, matter (pudgala) persists as a substance while its forms, combinations, and configurations vary.

Within the framework of the Jain standpoints, dravyanaya is often contrasted with paryāyanaya, the modal standpoint. While paryāyanaya focuses on specific, momentary states or modes of a substance (such as being hot, cold, moving, or resting), dravyanaya focuses on the substance as the bearer of these modes. Both standpoints are considered valid but partial: each captures a different aspect of the same reality. Anekāntavāda insists that a complete understanding of any entity requires integrating these standpoints rather than absolutizing one of them.

Technically, the substantial standpoint is closely tied to the definition of substance found in classical Jain texts. Substance is defined as that which possesses qualities and modes (guṇaparyayavat dravyam), and also as that which is characterized by origination (utpāda), destruction (vyaya), and permanence (dhrauvya). From the substantial standpoint, permanence (dhrauvya) is foregrounded: the entity is seen as a continuing reality that underlies the succession of origination and destruction of particular modes. This does not deny change; rather, it frames change as occurring within the enduring identity of the substance.

In practical and ethical contexts, the substantial standpoint supports the Jain emphasis on the enduring moral and spiritual responsibility of the soul. Actions (karma) may be momentary modes, but they leave lasting impressions on the soul-substance. The soul’s capacity for knowledge, faith, and conduct is treated as an essential quality, even when obscured by karmic bondage. Thus, dravyanaya underlies the conviction that liberation (mokṣa) is possible: the soul’s true nature as pure, conscious substance can be realized by removing obstructing modes (karmic paryāya) rather than by annihilating the soul itself.

Philosophically, the substantial standpoint also functions as a corrective to one-sided views that either absolutize permanence (ignoring change) or absolutize change (denying enduring identity). Jain thinkers argue that some non-Jain schools fall into these extremes—either positing a single, unchanging absolute or denying substantial reality altogether. Dravyanaya allows Jainism to affirm both continuity and transformation: substances are real and enduring, yet their modes are genuinely diverse and changing. This balanced view is central to Jain ontology, cosmology, and soteriology.

Modern interpreters often highlight that the substantial standpoint is not meant to be a dogmatic claim that only substances matter; rather, it is a methodological lens. When one asks what something really is, dravyanaya answers in terms of its basic kind and essential qualities. When one asks how it is at a particular time or in a particular relation, paryāyanaya answers in terms of its modes. Together, these standpoints help avoid simplistic metaphysical claims and encourage a nuanced, many-sided understanding of reality, consistent with the Jain commitment to intellectual non-violence and careful speech.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (Tattvārthādhigama)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāmī (Umāsvāti)
primary_sources.translation:
“Substance is that which possesses qualities and modes.”
“Existence is that which is characterized by origination, destruction, and permanence.”
primary_sources.notes: These aphorisms, found in the Tattvārthasūtra (commonly in the fifth chapter on substances), provide the foundational definition of dravya (substance) that underlies the substantial standpoint (dravyanaya). The first sūtra defines substance as the bearer of qualities (guṇa) and modes (paryāya), while the second describes the triple mark of existence: origination (utpāda), destruction (vyaya), and permanence (dhrauvya). Traditional commentaries such as Ācārya Pūjyapāda’s Sarvārthasiddhi elaborate that from the substantial standpoint, the focus is on permanence and the enduring identity of the substance, even as its modes arise and perish.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārthasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text: द्रव्यं गुणपर्यायाश्रयः । न हि गुणपर्यायवर्जितं द्रव्यं न च द्रव्यवर्जितो गुणपर्यायः ।
primary_sources.transliteration:
dravyaṃ guṇaparyāyāśrayaḥ.
na hi guṇaparyāyavarjitaṃ dravyaṃ na ca dravyavarjito guṇaparyāyaḥ.
primary_sources.translation: “Substance is the substratum of qualities and modes. For there is no substance devoid of qualities and modes, nor are there qualities and modes without substance.”
primary_sources.notes: In this classical Digambara commentary, Pūjyapāda clarifies the inseparable relation between substance, qualities, and modes. From the substantial standpoint, the substance is treated as the substratum that persists through the succession of modes. The passage emphasizes that neither substance nor its modes can exist independently, supporting the Jain view that dravyanaya and paryāyanaya are complementary standpoints on the same reality rather than descriptions of separate entities.

primary_sources.title: Nayāvatāra (Treatise on Standpoints)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Siddhasena Divākara
primary_sources.translation: “The substantial standpoint is the observation of the enduring aspect, whereas the modal standpoint is the observation of the momentary aspect.”
primary_sources.notes: Although wording varies across manuscripts and editions, Siddhasena’s Nayāvatāra is a key source for the classification and explanation of Jain standpoints (naya). Here, dravyanaya is explicitly defined as the standpoint that attends to the enduring aspect (sthāyibhāva) of an entity, while paryāyanaya attends to its momentary aspect (kṣaṇikabhāva). This text is central for understanding how the substantial standpoint functions within the broader epistemological and logical framework of anekāntavāda.

misconceptions.myth: The substantial standpoint denies change and treats all things as completely static.
misconceptions.reality: The substantial standpoint does not deny change; it highlights the enduring identity of a substance while fully acknowledging that its modes arise and perish. Jain texts explicitly define substance as that which possesses qualities and modes and is characterized by origination, destruction, and permanence. Dravyanaya focuses on permanence and continuity, but it is always paired with modal standpoints that describe change.

misconceptions.myth: From the substantial standpoint, only substances are real and modes are illusory or unreal.
misconceptions.reality: Jain philosophy affirms the reality of both substances and their modes. Modes are genuine states of a substance, not illusions. The substantial standpoint emphasizes the substance as the bearer of these modes, but it does not deny their reality. Instead, it insists that modes cannot exist without a substance, and a substance cannot exist without modes, making both aspects integral to a complete account of reality.

misconceptions.myth: The substantial standpoint is the only correct viewpoint, and other standpoints are inferior or mistaken.
misconceptions.reality: Within anekāntavāda, no single standpoint is considered absolutely complete. The substantial standpoint is valid but partial, just like the modal and other standpoints. Jain thinkers stress that a comprehensive understanding of reality requires integrating multiple standpoints. Absolutizing dravyanaya alone would itself be a form of one-sidedness (ekānta), which Jainism explicitly rejects.

misconceptions.myth: The substantial standpoint is purely theoretical and has no relevance for spiritual practice.
misconceptions.reality: The substantial standpoint has direct implications for spiritual practice. By emphasizing the enduring nature and essential qualities of the soul-substance, it supports the conviction that liberation is possible and that the soul’s true nature is pure, conscious, and capable of right faith, knowledge, and conduct. Ethical and meditative disciplines are understood as ways of transforming the soul’s modes and removing karmic obstructions, not as attempts to destroy the soul itself.
